covered: Cash and cash-equivalent criteria; maturity measured from acquisition; liquidity versus price risk; reported cash versus amounts usable for a decision; internal transfers.
deferred: Overdraft exceptions, foreign-exchange translation, fund-specific valuation, complete current/non-current presentation, local adoption and tax rules.

hoverDefinition: Cash includes cash on hand and demand deposits. A cash equivalent must be readily convertible to a known amount with insignificant value risk, and be held to meet short-term cash commitments.

objectives.statement: Classify balances using stated purpose, liquidity, maturity and value-risk facts.
objectives.evidence: Exclude receivables and investments that fail the cash-equivalent conditions.

objectives.statement: Separate reported cash from amounts available after a stated use restriction.
objectives.evidence: Reconcile restricted amounts and explain why a qualifying internal transfer does not create cash flow.

context.timeframe: A separate illustrative teaching month. Every worked example and practice scenario starts independently; these are not consecutive company-case rounds.
assumptions: Eligibility and risk characteristics are supplied explicitly for the teaching instruments.
The stated restriction leaves the nature of the demand deposit unchanged but prevents the assessed use.
The management buffer is hypothetical; no borrowing netting, taxes or currency effects.

framework.name: IAS 7 under IFRS Accounting Standards, introductory reference
framework.jurisdiction: International IFRS reference; local adoption and Indian reporting requirements not assessed
framework.period: Public reference material checked 19 October 2026; this is not an entity reporting-period compliance opinion
framework.limitations: Focus on component definitions and stated eligibility facts. No claim to cover all classification exceptions, jurisdictional adoption, or IFRS 18 effective-date consequences.

abbreviations.definition: Cash and cash equivalents: the eligible combined balance, not all current assets.

mechanism.title: Distinguish money from a claim to future money
paragraphs: Cash on hand and bank demand deposits are cash. A trade receivable is a claim on a customer, not a bank balance. Inventory and equipment are also resources, but they cannot be spent as cash without another transaction. Profit is a period’s accounting performance, not a cash asset.
Read the component note rather than assuming that every balance labelled short-term investment is cash. The business should also reconcile reported cash components to the statement of cash flows.

mechanism.title: Apply all the cash-equivalent conditions
paragraphs: A candidate investment must be held to meet short-term cash commitments, be highly liquid, convert readily to a known amount and have insignificant risk of changes in value. A short maturity supports these conditions; under IAS 7 it is normally, for example, three months or less measured from acquisition. Maturity alone is not sufficient.

A twelve-month investment bought at issue does not become a cash equivalent merely because only two months remain at the reporting date. Daily redeemability alone does not make a price-sensitive fund a cash equivalent. Assess the instrument’s substance, purpose and risk rather than its marketing name.

mechanism.title: Check whether the reported balance can fund this decision
paragraphs: Accounting inclusion and operational availability are distinct questions. A contractual use restriction does not automatically remove a demand deposit from cash if its nature is unchanged. Nevertheless the amount might not be usable for a particular supplier payment. Identify the actual restriction and state the decision perimeter.

After removing amounts unavailable for the decision, a manager may also retain an explicitly assumed minimum buffer. A buffer is a management policy, not an accounting reclassification. The remainder is not automatically distributable or excess cash for valuation: upcoming commitments, debt terms and other constraints still matter.

mechanism.title: Do not invent a cash inflow from an internal transfer
paragraphs: Moving money between a demand account and a qualifying cash equivalent changes the components but not their combined total. It is not an external cash flow in the cash-flow statement. A purchase of an investment that does not qualify is different and must be classified under the relevant reporting requirements.

distinctions.name: Cash and cash equivalents
distinctions.explanation: Demand money is cash; only investments satisfying all the stated conditions are equivalents.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Do not classify solely by the number of months on a label.

distinctions.name: Acquisition maturity and remaining maturity
distinctions.explanation: The normal short-maturity assessment is from acquisition, not merely the balance-sheet date.
distinctions.whenItMatters: A long investment does not gradually reclassify just because its maturity approaches.

distinctions.name: Liquidity and insignificant price risk
distinctions.explanation: An investment can be easy to sell but still change materially in price.
distinctions.whenItMatters: A daily redemption facility is insufficient on its own.

distinctions.name: Reported and usable cash
distinctions.explanation: Some included balances can have restrictions relevant to a specific decision.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Avoid both overstating operational liquidity and automatically excluding every restricted deposit from reported cash.

distinctions.name: Buffer and accounting classification
distinctions.explanation: A chosen minimum-cash buffer is a decision assumption.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Keep the liquidity policy visible instead of treating it as a reporting rule.

distinctions.name: Cash stock and period flow
distinctions.explanation: The closing balance is a stock; receipts and payments explain its period movement.
distinctions.whenItMatters: Do not add closing cash to period income or count internal transfers as receipts.

workedExample.setup: Separate balance-date illustration: Nila has physical cash 1, a demand deposit 14 (including 4 subject to a supplier-use restriction that does not change its demand nature), a qualifying treasury bill 6 acquired with two months to maturity and held for near-term payments, a non-qualifying investment 5 acquired with twelve months to maturity, receivables 8 and inventory 7. The treasury bill is readily convertible to a known amount with insignificant value risk. The restriction makes 4 unavailable for the decision under review. Assume a management buffer of 3.
steps: Cash = physical cash 1 + demand deposit 14 = 15. The restricted portion is already inside the 14; do not add it again.
The supplied treasury-bill facts satisfy the cash-equivalent conditions, so add 6. Reported cash and cash equivalents = 21.
Exclude the longer investment 5, customer receivables 8 and inventory 7. This classification does not say those other assets have zero value.
For the specific payment decision, usable cash and equivalents = 21 − unavailable amount 4 = 17.
Amount above the assumed management buffer = 17 − 3 = 14. It is not automatically distributable or valuation excess cash.
Moving 2 from the unrestricted demand deposit into another qualifying bill reduces one component by 2 and raises another by 2. The combined reported balance remains 21.
workedExample.result: Reported cash and equivalents: 21. Usable for the stated decision: 17. Above the assumed buffer: 14.
workedExample.interpretation: The same accounts answer classification and liquidity questions differently. State whether a decision uses reported balances, usable balances or a buffer-adjusted amount.

statementEffects.explanation: This is a balance classification and liquidity exercise, not revenue recognition or a forecast of future receipts.
changes: Balance sheet: group cash and qualifying equivalents 21 under the stated IFRS reference assumptions; other assets remain outside that group.
Income statement: the classification or qualifying internal transfer creates no revenue or profit in this illustration.
Cash flow: an internal movement between cash and a qualifying equivalent is excluded from cash flows; total cash and equivalents do not change.

misconceptions.claim: Every current asset or sellable investment is cash.
misconceptions.correction: Apply cash-equivalent conditions and exclude customer claims and stock.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Can the amount be spent without collection or a price-risk-bearing sale?

misconceptions.claim: Any item close to maturity or redeemable daily must be a cash equivalent.
misconceptions.correction: Check acquisition maturity, purpose, liquidity, known amount and value risk together.
misconceptions.diagnostic: What could change the amount realised?

misconceptions.claim: Every reported cash amount is available for any decision.
misconceptions.correction: Assess restrictions and any stated management buffer separately.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Which commitment can this balance legally or operationally fund?

practice.setup: Separate scenario: demand deposit 7; bill 4 acquired with two months to maturity, held for short-term payments, readily convertible to a known amount with insignificant value risk; trade receivables 6. No other balances or restrictions.
practice.question: What is the reported cash-and-equivalent total?

options.feedback: Customer receivables still require collection; they are not cash.
The bill meets all supplied cash-equivalent conditions.
Cash 7 plus the qualifying bill 4 gives 11.

practice.solution: Reported cash and equivalents = 7 + 4 = 11. Exclude receivables 6.

hints.text: Check each component against the definition rather than grouping all current assets.
Reported cash and equivalents = 7 + 4 = 11. Exclude receivables 6.

reflection.prompt: Why is the customer balance treated differently from the bill?

practice.setup: Separate scenario: a demand deposit is 10, including 4 subject to a restriction that leaves its demand nature unchanged but prevents use for the payment being assessed. A qualifying bill is 3. A daily redeemable fund is 5 but its redemption value can vary materially. There are no other balances or buffers.
practice.question: Which reported and usable totals follow, before any other commitments?

options.feedback: The deposit remains cash under the stated facts, the bill qualifies, and 4 is unavailable for this decision.
Daily redemption does not overcome the fund’s material value risk.
The restriction affects this use but is explicitly assumed not to change the deposit’s cash nature.

practice.solution: Reported total = deposit 10 + bill 3 = 13. Usable for this decision = 13 − restricted portion 4 = 9. Exclude the price-sensitive fund. A subsequent transfer between eligible components would not change the combined 13.

hints.text: Separate the definition test from the restriction on a particular use.

Reported total = deposit 10 + bill 3 = 13. Usable for this decision = 13 − restricted portion 4 = 9. Exclude the price-sensitive fund. A subsequent transfer between eligible components would not change the combined 13.

reflection.prompt: Why can a balance remain cash while being unavailable for this payment?
